en.title: Persuasion
en.author: Jane Austen
en.summary: Persuaded at nineteen to give up the man she loved, Anne Elliot meets him again eight years later and learns to trust her own judgement.
en.notice: Sample content: the comments on this storyline were drafted by Claude as placeholders; replace them with your own. Quotations follow the Project Gutenberg text.
closing: Persuasion is a story about a second chance, but its real subject is judgement: the same woman listens to someone else at nineteen and to herself at twenty-seven.
Austen never turns the adviser into a villain, and never makes Anne regret obeying her. She simply lets time show that judgement is something a person grows into.

paragraphs: Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot's character; vanity of person and of situation.
...her word had no weight, her convenience was always to give way—she was only Anne.

blocks.text: The book opens on the father's mirror, then on the daughter's silence. "Only Anne" puts the heroine where she can barely be heard. The whole novel is that voice slowly growing louder.

paragraphs: She was persuaded to believe the engagement a wrong thing: indiscreet, improper, hardly capable of success, and not deserving it.
She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning.

blocks.text: The title lives here. Lady Russell is no villain; she truly wants the best for Anne, which is exactly why her advice is so hard to resist. Austen is not asking who was wrong, but what happens when someone without judgement of her own borrows another's.

paragraphs: Eight years, almost eight years had passed, since all had been given up.
You were so altered he should not have known you again.

blocks.text: Wentworth comes back rich, admired and still angry. Mary passes the remark on carelessly, yet it is the most painful line in the book. Anne does not argue, because she thinks the same.

paragraphs: Let those who would be happy be firm.
...a beautiful glossy nut, which, blessed with original strength, has outlived all the storms of autumn.

blocks.text: He is talking to Louisa, but every word lands on Anne, hidden behind the hedgerow. He holds firmness up as the highest virtue and reads Anne's old obedience as weakness. Two chapters later, Austen makes that firmness pay.

paragraphs: ...she was too precipitate by half a second, she fell on the pavement on the Lower Cobb, and was taken up lifeless!
"Is there no one to help me?"

blocks.text: Louisa's firmness turns out to be wilfulness. In the panic, the first person to think clearly is Anne, the one supposedly too easily persuaded. For the first time Wentworth sees that firmness and stubbornness are not the same thing.

paragraphs: Mr Elliot is a man without heart or conscience; a designing, wary, cold-blooded being, who thinks only of himself...
Oh! he is black at heart, hollow and black!

blocks.text: This is the second persuasion. Lady Russell admires the polished Mr Elliot and hopes Anne will marry him. This time Anne is not pushed along: she watches, listens, and goes to her old friend Mrs Smith for the truth.

nodes.title: The letter at the White Hart
nodes.label: Chapter 23

paragraphs: All the privilege I claim for my own sex... is that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone.
You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope.

blocks.text: Anne talks to Captain Harville, but speaks for Wentworth to hear; Wentworth writes a letter at the next table, for Anne to read. Each finally says, in their own way, what went unsaid for eight years. It is the quietest scene in the book, and the most intense.

paragraphs: ...I was right in submitting to her, and that if I had done otherwise, I should have suffered more in continuing the engagement than I did even in giving it up...
She gloried in being a sailor's wife, but she must pay the tax of quick alarm for belonging to that profession...

blocks.text: Anne does not say she was wrong; she says she had no better choice then. And the last line is not a fairy-tale "happily ever after" but happiness with worry inside it. Austen gives her love, and reality with it.

zh.title: 劝导
zh.author: 简·奥斯汀
zh.summary: 十九岁时被劝说放弃了爱情的安妮，在八年后与旧爱重逢，终于学会相信自己的判断。
zh.notice: 示例内容：故事线中的评论由 Claude 临时撰写，请替换成你自己的评论。原文引自 Project Gutenberg 版，中文为自译。
closing: 《劝导》讲的是第二次机会，但它真正的主题是“判断”：同一个人，在十九岁时听从别人，在二十七岁时听从自己。
奥斯汀没有把劝她的人写成坏人，也没有让安妮后悔服从。她只是让时间证明：一个人的判断，是可以慢慢长出来的。

paragraphs: Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot's character; vanity of person and of situation.
虚荣，是沃尔特·艾略特爵士性格的开头和结尾：对相貌的虚荣，也对地位的虚荣。
...her word had no weight, her convenience was always to give way—she was only Anne.
……她的话没有分量，她的方便总要让路——她只是安妮。

blocks.text: 开篇先写父亲的镜子，再写女儿的沉默。“只是安妮”四个字，把主角放在了一个几乎听不见声音的位置。整本书，就是这个声音慢慢变大的过程。

paragraphs: She was persuaded to believe the engagement a wrong thing: indiscreet, improper, hardly capable of success, and not deserving it.
她被劝说相信，这门婚约是错的：轻率、不合适、几乎不可能成功，也不值得坚持。
She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning.
年轻时她被迫学会了谨慎，年纪渐长才学会了浪漫：一个不自然的开头，自然会有这样的续篇。

blocks.text: 书名就藏在这里。劝她的拉塞尔夫人并不是坏人，她真心为安妮着想，所以这份劝说才更难反抗。奥斯汀写的不是“谁错了”，而是“一个人还没有判断力时，会把别人的判断当成自己的”。

paragraphs: Eight years, almost eight years had passed, since all had been given up.
八年，将近八年过去了，自从一切被放弃以后。
You were so altered he should not have known you again.
你变得太多了，他都认不出你了。

blocks.text: 温特沃斯回来了，有钱、有名，而且还在生气。这句话是妹妹玛丽随口转述的，却是全书最疼的一句。安妮没有反驳，因为她自己也这么想。

paragraphs: Let those who would be happy be firm.
想要幸福的人，就要坚定。
...a beautiful glossy nut, which, blessed with original strength, has outlived all the storms of autumn.
……一颗漂亮光亮的坚果，凭着天生的结实，熬过了整个秋天的风暴。

blocks.text: 他是在对路易莎说话，可每一句都落在躲在树篱后面的安妮身上。他把“坚定”当成最高的美德，把安妮当年的顺从当成软弱。两章之后，奥斯汀就让这种“坚定”付出了代价。

paragraphs: ...she was too precipitate by half a second, she fell on the pavement on the Lower Cobb, and was taken up lifeless!
……她早跳了半秒，摔在下科布的石板上，被扶起来时已经没有知觉！
"Is there no one to help me?"
“就没有人能帮我吗？”

blocks.text: 路易莎的“坚定”其实是任性。慌乱中第一个冷静下来、知道该做什么的，是那个被认为“太容易被说服”的安妮。温特沃斯在这一刻第一次看清：坚定和固执不是一回事。

paragraphs: Mr Elliot is a man without heart or conscience; a designing, wary, cold-blooded being, who thinks only of himself...
艾略特先生是一个没有心肝、没有良知的人；工于心计、处处提防、冷血，只想着他自己……
Oh! he is black at heart, hollow and black!
噢！他的心是黑的，空的，黑的！

blocks.text: 这是第二次“劝导”。拉塞尔夫人很看好风度翩翩的艾略特先生，希望安妮嫁给他。可这一次安妮没有被推着走，她自己去看，去听，去找老朋友史密斯太太问清真相。

paragraphs: All the privilege I claim for my own sex... is that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone.
我为我们女性所要求的唯一特权……就是在生命或希望都已不在的时候，爱得最久。
You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope.
你刺穿了我的灵魂。我一半是痛苦，一半是希望。

blocks.text: 安妮在和哈维尔上校聊天，话是说给温特沃斯听的；温特沃斯在一旁写信，信是写给安妮看的。两个人终于用各自的方式，把八年没说的话说了出来。这是全书最安静，也最激烈的一场戏。

paragraphs: ...I was right in submitting to her, and that if I had done otherwise, I should have suffered more in continuing the engagement than I did even in giving it up...
……我服从她是对的；如果当时我不那样做，坚持婚约给我带来的痛苦，会比放弃它还要多……
She gloried in being a sailor's wife, but she must pay the tax of quick alarm for belonging to that profession...
她以做一名海军军官的妻子为荣，但也必须为属于这个职业，付出随时担惊受怕的代价……

blocks.text: 安妮没有说自己当年错了，她说的是“我当时没有别的选择”。最后一句也不是童话式的“从此幸福”，而是幸福里带着担心。奥斯汀给了她爱情，也给了她现实。
